clue.text: Watch over third of Penelope Cruz covers

indicators.note: A cover lies over a thing on both sides, so the name named next is wrapped round the letter.

parts.note: the Cruz wanted is Ted, the Texas senator, not the actor the surface offers

indicators.note: 'Third of' counts along the letters of the name beside it and stops on the third one.

parts.note: the third letter of the name, counting from the front

explanation.surface: A film star's magazine covers, with somebody keeping an eye on them.
explanation.walkthrough: Two Cruzes are in play and the clue leans on the wrong one: Penelope is there for the surface, Ted is there for his letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To tend someone is to watch over them, the nursing sense of the verb rather than the tending that means to lean a certain way.

clue.text: Batter, work Frenchman over

parts.note: OP is short for opus, a work

indicators.note: in a down clue, over means the name is turned upside down, read backwards

parts.note: Rene is a typical French man's name

explanation.surface: An instruction to beat up a Frenchman, with 'batter' read as a verb.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Batter' looks like a verb but is a cricket noun: an opener is a batsman who goes in first.
explanation.definitionFit: In cricket an opener is one of the two batsmen who start the innings, so a batter.

clue.text: Run out of tent seized by darn crazy hysteric

indicators.note: the shortened tent is held inside the rearranged letters
crazy suggests the letters of darn go wild and are rearranged
Run is taken out of the tent word, so its letter is removed

parts.note: a marquee is a large tent
R is the cricket abbreviation for run

explanation.surface: Someone who runs out of a tent and is grabbed by a frantic person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Run' looks like a verb in the surface, but it is the cricket R; the jumbled darn wraps round what is left of the tent, its first three letters before and N after.
explanation.definitionFit: A drama queen is an informal term for a person given to overly emotional, theatrical reactions.

clue.text: Military standard unveiled by East Wing

indicators.note: with its covering stripped off, the word loses its outer letters

parts.note: a banner is a military standard or flag
X is the multiplication sign, read as 'by' (three by four)
E is the compass abbreviation for East

explanation.surface: A regimental flag revealed in the east wing of a building.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unveiled' strips the outer letters from BANNER to leave ANNE; 'by' is X as in measurements like 3 by 4.
explanation.definitionFit: An annexe is an extension built on to a main building, which is what a wing is.

clue.text: The Times: Oysters Turned Up Outside Sam's Home

indicators.note: Turned up, and a down entry read from the bottom of the grid upwards runs against the letters as printed.
'Outside' points at letters lying across the outer edges of the words rather than tucked away inside any one of them.

parts.note: eight consecutive letters starting on the last letter of the first word and stopping two into the last, running the wrong way

explanation.surface: A newspaper item about oysters, dug up from somewhere near Sam's house.
explanation.walkthrough: Capital letters on every word is Hat's camouflage: they make the clue look like a headline so that the join between 'The' and 'Times' never gets read as a join. Yosemite Sam is the cartoon gunslinger.
explanation.definitionFit: Yosemite Sam of the Looney Tunes cartoons takes his name from the California national park, so the definition asks for the place behind the name.

clue.text: A congested city rises again

indicators.note: in a down clue, rising means the word is read from bottom to top, backwards

parts.note: the Great Wen was a nickname for overcrowded London, so a wen is a congested city

explanation.surface: A crowded city springing up once more.
explanation.walkthrough: A wen is literally a swelling; William Cobbett called London 'the Great Wen'.
explanation.definitionFit: Anew and again both mean once more, starting a second time.

clue.text: Judi exhausted, carried by terribly skinny chap in tights

indicators.note: the emptied name is held inside the rearranged letters
terribly signals that the letters of skinny are badly jumbled
an exhausted thing is emptied out, so Judi keeps only its outer letters

parts.note: the name is the source of the letters here

explanation.surface: An exhausted Judi being carried by a thin man in tights.
explanation.walkthrough: Vaslav Nijinsky was a famous Russian ballet star; 'chap in tights' points to a male dancer, and Judi's two outer letters sit after the first two of the jumbled skinny.
explanation.definitionFit: Nijinsky was the celebrated Russian ballet dancer, and male dancers perform in tights.

clue.text: Welshman's platform

parts.note: Dai, short for Dafydd, is the crossword's stock Welshman
the possessive ending is taken as a letter of the answer

explanation.surface: A Welshman with a platform to speak from.
explanation.walkthrough: Two words, and one of them is an apostrophe: the possessive s is not grammar joining the halves of the clue but the last letter of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A dais is the low platform a speaker or a top table stands on, raised just enough to be seen from the back of the room.

clue.text: 2 sat wagging tongue

indicators.note: A wagging tongue swings from side to side, and letters that will not stay still are letters being reordered.

parts.note: the numeral sends you to the answer at 2 down, which supplies six of the letters
three more letters, taken as written

explanation.surface: Two people sitting there with their tongues wagging.
explanation.walkthrough: A bare number in a Guardian clue points at another entry, so this one cannot be started until 2 down is in — and it reads as 'two sat', which is the joke.
explanation.definitionFit: A tongue is a language, and Esperanto is the invented one, so the definition uses the broad sense rather than the thing in your mouth.

clue.text: West African rhino has Unitarian retreating

indicators.note: 'Has' is the loosest word here: it says the money holds these letters, with the word order stretched to keep the surface upright.
A retreat is a going back the way you came, and in an across entry that means right to left.

parts.note: five consecutive letters at the tail of the word, waiting to be turned round

explanation.surface: A rhino in West Africa backing away from a passing Unitarian.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rhino' for money is Victorian slang the crossword keeps alive, and the surface protects it by making the animal West African too.
explanation.definitionFit: Rhino is old British slang for cash, and the naira is Nigeria's currency, so the definition asks for West African money.

clue.text: Material taken from ground from the east

indicators.note: Something coming from the east travels westwards, and in an across entry that is right to left.

parts.note: what has been dug out of the ground has been mined

explanation.surface: Ore dug out of the ground somewhere east of here.
explanation.walkthrough: The word 'from' turns up twice doing different jobs — once as part of the digging, once as the instruction — which is what makes the turn hard to spot.
explanation.definitionFit: Denim is the heavy cotton twill jeans are cut from, so 'material' is a plain fabric synonym with no colour in it.

clue.text: White flower displayed by Wise when playing with Leeds

indicators.note: Letters caught at play are letters off duty, and off-duty letters do not stay in the positions they were given.

parts.note: anagram fodder, four letters
anagram fodder, five more

explanation.surface: A footballer called Wise showing off a bit of skill in a Leeds shirt.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the first two words have anything to do with botany; the rest reads as a team sheet, which is where nine letters sit in plain view.
explanation.definitionFit: Edelweiss is the woolly white daisy of the high Alps, so the definition names it by its colour and its kind.

clue.text: Extravagantly ornate vessel loaded with cargo at the back

indicators.note: the ship has the letter put inside it, like freight in a hold

parts.note: a barque is a sailing ship

indicators.note: at the back points to the final letter of cargo

parts.note: supplies its final letter

explanation.surface: A richly decorated ship with goods stowed at its stern.
explanation.walkthrough: 'at the back' gives O, the last letter of cargo, and 'loaded with' puts it inside BARQUE.
explanation.definitionFit: Baroque describes the highly elaborate, decorative style of seventeenth-century art and architecture.

clue.text: Low character, Liberal, one probing British parliamentarian

indicators.note: A probe goes into the thing it examines, so these letters push in among the others rather than sitting beside them.

parts.note: standard abbreviation
a member of parliament
standard abbreviation, as on a ballot paper
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Somebody of low character digging into the affairs of a British MP.
explanation.walkthrough: Low is a surname, not an adjective: David Low drew Colonel Blimp for the papers in the 1930s, and the walrus-moustached old reactionary has been a byword since.
explanation.definitionFit: Colonel Blimp is the pompous reactionary drawn by David Low, so 'Low character' means a character belonging to the cartoonist Low.

clue.text: Popular sibling without hesitation beginning to suggest demands

parts.note: in means fashionable or popular

indicators.note: the hesitation is taken away from the sibling word

parts.note: a sister is a sibling
er is the sound of hesitating

indicators.note: the beginning of suggest means its opening letter

parts.note: supplies its first letter

explanation.surface: A well-liked sibling who, without pausing, starts to make suggestions and demands.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' removes ER from SISTER to leave SIST; 'beginning to' gives S from suggest.
explanation.definitionFit: To insist is to demand firmly, so insists works as a verb meaning demands.

clue.text: Vegas's last crook gambler

indicators.note: 'Last' asks for the final letter of the word standing in front of it, and nothing else of it.

parts.note: the closing letter of the city's name
to peculate is to embezzle money you were trusted with, so a peculator is a crook

explanation.surface: The last crook to get out of Las Vegas.
explanation.walkthrough: Peculator is the rare word to learn — an embezzler — and the Vegas surface is built so that every other word is already about money and cheating.
explanation.definitionFit: A speculator gambles on shares, land or currency rather than cards, so 'gambler' catches the money-market sense of the word.

clue.text: French barman posed, tied, naked

parts.note: to pose for a portrait is to sit for it

indicators.note: Something naked has lost what covered it, so the word beside it gives up the letters at both ends.

parts.note: the word 'tied' with its outer letters stripped off

explanation.surface: A French barman who posed for a photograph tied up and with nothing on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Barman' is the joke and the definition at once: not a man behind a bar but a man who works in bars, which is what a composer does all day.
explanation.definitionFit: Music is written in bars, so a composer can be called a barman, and the French one the letters build is Erik Satie.

clue.text: Hat is miserable, lacking will ultimately to inspire

indicators.note: the phrase is missing that letter

parts.note: Hat is the setter, so 'Hat is' is I'M
blue means sad or miserable

indicators.note: ultimately points to the final letter of will

parts.note: supplies its last letter

explanation.surface: The setter confesses to being unhappy and short of the will to inspire others.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter's pseudonym is Hat, so 'Hat is' gives I'M; I'M BLUE 'lacking' L (last of 'will') leaves IMBUE.
explanation.definitionFit: To imbue is to fill someone with a feeling or quality, much as to inspire them.

clue.text: Nick rolled over, rolled over topless in brothel

indicators.note: rolled over means turned backwards, so the word reads in reverse

parts.note: to nick is to steal or rob

indicators.note: over turns what remains upside down in this down clue
topless removes the word's first letter

parts.note: the second 'rolled' is the fodder

explanation.surface: A thief in a brothel who rolled over and over without a top on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rolled over' turns ROB into BOR; the second 'rolled', 'topless', loses R to give OLLED, which 'over' turns into DELLO.
explanation.definitionFit: Bordello is an Italian-derived synonym for a house of prostitution.

clue.text: Regularly offered payment

indicators.note: Doing something regularly is doing it at a fixed interval, so letters are taken at every second position.

parts.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters of the word, read in order

explanation.surface: A payment that gets offered on a regular basis.
explanation.walkthrough: Three-letter answers give you almost nothing to aim at, so the instruction has to be found first — and only one word here is long enough to hide a run of alternate letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A fee is what a professional charges for a service — a solicitor's or a doctor's payment, agreed in advance rather than earned by the hour.

clue.text: Corporal perhaps put on fine, shiny material for dance

indicators.note: 'Put on' is loose about position: it adds the officer to the other pieces without saying which end he goes.

parts.note: F is the pencil grade meaning fine
lame is cloth woven through with metallic thread
a corporal is one rank of non-commissioned officer, and 'perhaps' flags the example

explanation.surface: A corporal turned out in something fine and shiny for a dance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Corporal perhaps' points the opposite way from most definitions by example: the rank is the instance and the abbreviation for the category is what you write down.
explanation.definitionFit: Flamenco is the Andalusian dance of stamping heels and clapped rhythm, so the bare word 'dance' is a broad but honest synonym.

clue.text: Torture admitted by alien nation

indicators.note: To admit someone is to let them in, so the alien takes the other letters inside itself.

parts.note: ET, the film's extra-terrestrial, is the crossword's standard alien
gyp is British for sharp pain — a bad knee gives you gyp

explanation.surface: An alien owning up to torture.
explanation.walkthrough: Nothing in the surface is remotely geographical, which is why the last word reads as part of the story rather than as the definition standing on its own.
explanation.definitionFit: Egypt is a country, so 'nation' is about as plain a synonym as a definition gets — the work is in seeing where the definition starts.

clue.text: Quiet country hotel, first-class fish

parts.note: p is piano, the musical direction to play quietly
a country, taken whole
H is hotel in the NATO alphabet
first-class work is graded A

explanation.surface: A quiet, first-class country hotel.
explanation.walkthrough: Three single letters come from standing conventions and the fourth piece is a country sitting in plain sight, while the surface reads as a line from a hotel review.
explanation.definitionFit: The piranha is the South American river fish with the notorious teeth, so 'fish' defines it by the family it belongs to.

clue.text: Last slice of Arctic roll for pud

indicators.note: A slice off the end of a word is one letter, and the end meant here is the far one.

parts.note: the closing letter of the word 'Arctic'
thunder rolls, that is, it rumbles

explanation.surface: The last slice of an Arctic roll, served up for pudding.
explanation.walkthrough: An Arctic roll is a British ice-cream pudding in a sponge sleeve, so the surface offers one dessert while the definition quietly asks for another.
explanation.definitionFit: A crumble is baked fruit under a rubbly flour-and-butter topping, and pud is the British shorthand for the sweet course.

clue.text: Republican supporting Tory Party high flier

indicators.note: What supports a thing sits underneath it, and in a down entry underneath means later in the answer.

parts.note: Con is how the Conservative party appears on a British ballot paper
a do is a party, a bash
standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: An American Republican backing the Tory party.
explanation.walkthrough: Both political words are letters rather than politics, and 'Party' with its capital is the one to distrust: it is the party you go to, not the party you vote for.
explanation.definitionFit: The condor is the Andean vulture that soars higher than almost any bird, so 'high flier' is meant literally rather than as the ambitious-person idiom.

clue.text: £1 filled Chinese bun pintxos sold here

indicators.note: 'Filled' does double duty: it describes the bun on the surface and puts one set of letters inside another underneath.

parts.note: a bao is the steamed Chinese bun
read the other way round as 1lb: I for one and lb for pound

explanation.surface: A filled Chinese bun going for a pound, next to the bar snacks.
explanation.walkthrough: Both pounds in this clue are the same word underneath — £ and lb each come from the Latin libra — which is the licence for reading £1 as 1lb.
explanation.definitionFit: Pintxos are Basque bar snacks pinned to a slice of bread, and Bilbao is the largest city of the Basque Country, where they are sold everywhere.

clue.text: Inexperienced head that's likely to get chopped

parts.note: green = raw, new to the job
bean is slang for the head, as in 'use your bean'

explanation.surface: A new boss who looks likely to be sacked before long.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the whole second half and it works by function rather than synonym: getting the chop is a sacking on the surface and a chopping board underneath.
explanation.definitionFit: A green bean is topped, tailed and chopped before it goes anywhere near a pan, so the definition names the vegetable by what the cook does to it.

clue.text: Stomach punched by second blow

indicators.note: A punch lands in the middle of what it hits, so the letter goes inside rather than alongside.

parts.note: the gut is the stomach
standard abbreviation for a second of time

explanation.surface: Someone taking a second punch to the stomach.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blow' is the trap: the surface has just landed a punch, and the definition means a rush of wind.
explanation.definitionFit: A gust is a blow of wind, using the noun sense of a sudden rush of air rather than the punch the surface has in mind.

clue.text: Average type, and not married

parts.note: nor is the one word that means exactly 'and not'
standard abbreviation, as on a form

explanation.surface: An average sort of person, and unmarried with it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'And not' looks like joinery or a negative instruction and is neither: it is a conjunction being defined, letter for letter, by its own meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: A norm is the standard that other things get measured against, so 'average type' asks for the ordinary run of things rather than a person.

clue.text: Broad-shouldered bloke getting time off finally

indicators.note: 'Off' takes away what has just been named, so the letter it follows never appears.

parts.note: finally can be said as 'at last', which is where the letters come from
T is the abbreviation for time, and this is the letter taken away

explanation.surface: A big bloke finally getting some time off work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Finally' is neither definition nor instruction but a phrase to be spelled out, and the Titan carrying the heavens is the broad-shouldered bloke of the first two words.
explanation.definitionFit: Atlas is the Titan condemned to hold up the sky, so any man built to carry a weight on his shoulders can be called one.

clue.text: For starters, some marinated eel with duck

indicators.note: 'For starters' asks for the letters that start the words while pretending to order the first course.

parts.note: the opening letters of four consecutive words, taken in order

explanation.surface: A starter of marinated eel, with duck to follow.
explanation.walkthrough: The menu runs top to bottom and 'with' is the word to watch: it looks like the joinery between two courses and is one of the four words donating a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The smew is a small white sawbill duck that winters on northern European lakes, so 'duck' names it by its family.

clue.text: Former garret, very large area, right?

parts.note: so = very, as in 'so kind of you'
L is the clothing size
standard abbreviation
standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: Somebody running through the details of an old attic room: very large, on the right.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Former' is a label rather than a piece of wordplay: a solar is the upper chamber of a medieval house, a word you meet in castles and never in an estate agent's window.
explanation.definitionFit: A solar was the private upper room of a medieval house, so 'former garret' asks for a room at the top in a word that is now only historical.

clue.text: Teach cool new Topic?

indicators.note: Something new is made afresh out of what was already there, and here that means the same letters in another order.

parts.note: anagram fodder, nine letters

explanation.surface: A teacher trying to make a subject sound cool and new.
explanation.walkthrough: Topic is the British chocolate bar advertised as having a hazelnut in every bite, and the question mark is the setter owning up: the definition is one example of the answer, not a synonym for it.
explanation.definitionFit: A Topic is a British hazelnut bar, so the definition hands over one brand and asks for the stuff it is made of — which the question mark flags.
